lines: This is the Commercial Workflow Leverage Lab, an independent concept by Ayo Ahmed.
Every company, person and number in it is synthetic.
I rank eight commercial workflows with one formula you can see and argue with.
Missing inputs stay unranked. Recruiter search is excluded, because that is the company's own product.
The sales to onboarding handoff leads on leverage per build day, by a clear margin.
I select it, and the choice is bound to these exact inputs.
Next, build versus buy.
Buying stays partly unscored, because cost and security are unknown. Even its upper bound can't beat a thin checker.
So I record the decision to build, owned by Business Operations.
On the handoff desk, every fact quotes its exact source.
Here, two sources disagree on the hiring system, so the packet abstains instead of guessing.
A person picks one of the cited values, and records the reason, so the choice can be audited.
This packet hides an instruction inside a synthetic call note.
It is quarantined as plain data, and it changes nothing.
Before approval, a packet needs one accountable owner from the CS roster,
and a dated adoption checkpoint, with a named metric and a threshold.
Approval is bound to a content fingerprint. Any later edit makes it stale.
Running it builds a simulated onboarding plan. Nothing is emailed, or written to a CRM.
The effort view compares synthetic baseline and assisted minutes, segment by segment.
Partial timers are excluded. A segment with no baseline is not compared, and none of it is called lift.
The rules export as a reusable operating playbook, with a full audit trail.
Finally, the evaluations. Sixteen expected and actual cases pass on the real rules.
Swap in a rule where the first source wins, and the contradiction cases turn red.
